title: Comment from Charles Gloor
comment_text:
The terminology used in the draft guidance is in my view not sufficiently descriptive of the challenges facing the use of HCT/Ps.

There is also the question of the use of autologous cells vs. allogeneic cells whether for adipose tissue or homologous us.

Autologous adipose tissue has been used by cosmetic surgeons for many years to "fill" areas on a patient using their own tissue.

Care must be taken when creating new guidances and regulation on the use of these types of tissues for treatment or study that may drive potentially useful therapies away from study and drive potentially harmful practices under ground, perhaps under the guise of "cosmetic surgery".

title: Comment from Arete-Zoe, LLC
comment_text:
Re: Comments on "Draft Guidances Relating to the Regulation of Human Cells, Tissues, or Cellular or Tissue-Based Products"

I wish to comment on the concerned draft guidance and propose introduction of certain measures that would facilitate informed decision-making by stakeholders involved. All participants in the system need reliable and accurate information to make better treatment decisions: patients who consider stem cell treatments, healthcare professionals who care for these patients before and after such treatment, and payers, who may or may not wish to include these therapies in their programs depending on their benefits, risks, and cost-effectiveness.

The Helsinki Declaration says on unproven Interventions in Clinical Practice:
37. In the treatment of an individual patient, where proven interventions do not exist or other known interventions have been ineffective, the physician, after seeking expert advice, with informed consent from the patient or a legally authorized representative, may use an unproven intervention if in the physician's judgement it offers hope of saving life, re-establishing health or alleviating suffering. This intervention should subsequently be made the object of research, designed to evaluate its safety and efficacy. In all cases, new information must be recorded and, where appropriate, made publicly available.

Most stem cell interventions are not reimbursed by insurers. Most of the time, patients have to pay for these treatments themselves. Patients are making decisions based on information they can find in public domain. Currently, it is very difficult to accurately evaluate the benefit:risk profile of stem cell treatments. Because procedures under 21 CFR part 1271 (CGTP) do not qualify as studies, treatment outcomes of these interventions are never made available to the public.
Interventions offered by establishments under 21 CFR part 1271 (CGTP) rely on studies that have already been done and published, as well as their own empirical experience from own medical practice. Brief overview of registered studies and published studies illustrate the scope and extent of the information gap on stem cell treatments and their outcomes.

Creation of a registry
To facilitate informed decision-making by patients, healthcare professionals, and insurers, I am suggesting creation of a registry into which information on stem cell interventions conducted under 21 CFR part 1271 would be reported. To make such undertaking worthwhile, the anonymized dataset would have to include indication, type of treatment, and treatment outcome. Not only this would greatly benefit patients, who would be able to make truly informed choice for themselves; this registry could also benefit healthcare professionals who would be able to compare stem cell interventions to other existing therapies.

In total, 5,298 studies conducted with stem cells globally as of January 7, 2016 (ClinicalTrials.gov). Most studies are conducted in highly regulated markets in the U.S. and in Europe. Other popular destinations include China, Iran, Israel and Middle America. (FIG 1)

The register lists wide variety of conditions studied in a manner that is difficult to assess. Many conditions are listed under wide variety of terms, often overlapping, some low level, and others very general and high level. It is therefore difficult to judge whether a study intervention should be at all included in a specific evaluation without detailed scrutiny of the study objectives and design. This task is challenging even for an experienced biomedical researcher, and virtually impossible for a non-healthcare professional.

Stem cell therapies potentially offer great benefits to patients whose current options are either limited or non-existent. Some patients are willing to undergo new, experimental and unproven therapies, to take advantage of this cutting-edge research. These people are taking all the risks associated with novel therapies and procedures upon themselves.
To protect the interests of patients, and to support innovation in this rapidly developing field of medicine, it would be wise to facilitate substantial improvement of the information environment, and to provide all parties involved with the information they need to make better treatment decisions.

title: Comment from Eliza Tyler
comment_text:
To Whom it May Concern;

My name is Eliza Tyler; I have lived with Type 1 Diabetes for 43 years.
I have had a multitude of treatments for various complications, several being pharmaceuticals which worked for a while and then abruptly removed from the market, i.e., Propulsid. I have also been rejected from the FDA/NIH backed clinical trial for islet cell transplant. That has not left me with a lot of options.

After over a year or more of research, looking for other options to extend my life with a better quality, I decided to undergo treatment with StemGenex. I am a firm believer in stem cell science and medicine. I know that an eventual cure will involve stem cells. From my research and my personal experience with the treatments, I have undergone three of these treatments thus far, I have had improved A1c levels, an improvement in many of the ongoing complications I have suffered, along with improved cognitive function from a brain injury suffered in 2011. One cannot deny the improvements, not even my following physicians.

The FDA approved a lot of drugs last year, did these all undergo scrupulous trials? My guess, is NO.

I believe that until the FDA, NIH, the US government and/or any other agencies put strict regulations on the right to use my own cells as a method of treatment that they do some serious consideration to those that these treatments have already shown to have improvements for. If these treatments are not allowed to come to us, the patients, the people who need them most, then this is only going to promote an increase in medical tourism. I considered it myself prior to locating the fine people at StemGenex.

PLEASE .... STOP THE MADNESS!!!!

These treatments are life saving for many, and hold the key to not only potential cures, but to a better quality of life from the devastating diseases which big pharma are only going to prolong, add more side effects and cause more pain and suffering.

I appreciate your consideration in bringing these and keeping these treatments, using my own cells, to the forefront and stop putting absurd road blocks in our way. I am all too aware of the fraud, and unscrupulous individuals who reside in our society, however, one must do their research. As a governing agency, I would like to think that you would allow the passionate and educated scientists who strive to bring these treatments to the people to do their jobs and not be persuaded by the big pharma dollars that have no doubt come to guide and rule this issue.

comment_text: I was diagnosed in 2006 with Rheumatoid Arthritis and tried Enbrel, Humira, Symponi, and Orencia combined with oral and Injectable steroids.  These all helped for a certain amount of time with many side effects with the biologics (increased infections mostly with the biologics) and numerous side effects with the steroids (weight gain, moodiness, exhaustion, irritation, overall a bad feeling) but none put me in what I would call "remission" until I went to Stemgenex in February of 2015.  In 2014 despite continued biologics (my 4th one) use and increased oral and injectable steroids my health detiorated and my labs were incresaing in value (not a good thing).  I was in a place of taking prescription pain medications (at night because I could not use them and work during the day) and was in constant pain-24 hours a day.  I was getting to a point where I was no longer able to work but that was not a realistic option.  My rheumatologist had reached her comfort level in prescribing biologics and I looked to the National Institute of Health.  That led me to studies being done on stemcell therapy using ones own fat cells.  That led me to Stemgenex in LaJolla California which literally saved my life.  I work in the pharmaceutical industry (biologics) and I am a very big supporter of them.  However, they do not work for everyone and I believe StemCell Therapy as a first line option is key to healing individuals such as myself and for the future of medicine.  The cost of one treatment was about the same as 3 months of therapy that my insurance company was paying for my biologics and other medicines.  Literally had I been able to try this therapy first instead of last my insurance and the system would have saved thousands of dollars a month they had been paying over the last 9 years.  Within 3 months of my therapy I was able to dose down/off all of my rheumatoid arthritis medicines-I only take hormones for age and synthroid for thyroid.  I am pain free and I have just celebrated my one year anniversary of my stem cell therapy by Stemgenex.  Without this therapy I am not sure where I would be today....I certainly know I would have been a greater cost to the system and my life would have Zero quality.  I wish you could hear me pleading with you to let this therapy not only remain an option but encourage an open this option for insurances to pay for it for individuals!  Thank you for considering this and I am happy to answer any questions!

comment_text: I want to comment in favor of Stem Cells.  My wife is now 59 and diagnosed at 50 with early onset by Mayo Clinic. She receives treatments in Panama with cells from umbilical cords of normal live births.  The donors are tested every month and my wife is tested prior to each treatment. comment_text:
In favor of Human Cell, tissue or Cellular based products

I was diagnosed with Primary Progressive Multiple Sclerosis in 2007, Therapies that were available for MS patients were only for those that had Relapsing-Remitting MS. I was told to prepare to be in a wheelchair in a matter of a few years, and there were no therapies or medications that could slow or inhibit the progression of my disease.
My treatment consisted of immune suppression therapy, and high doses of steroids every month. The side effects were horrendous, and my disease progressed.
I was 43 years old, a wife, and a mother of 2 children under the age of 6. I could hardly function, the fatigue and brain fog made daily living extremely difficult, and walking was becoming very limited. Imagine going from walking 3-5 miles a day to barely being able to get out of bed...and not able to take care of your children.
This was not acceptable to a person that had been fit and healthy all their life.
There had to be something that could help, the next year was spent doing extensive research on PPMS treatments. Ever where across the globe, stem cell therapies were being studied, and positive results were being seen. My husband and I decided that this was our only hope, and made the decision to have stem cell therapy. We knew and understood that this was not a cure, but a treatment that could possibly reset my immune system and alleviate my MS symptoms of extreme fatigue, brain fog, inability to stand or walk unassisted, and feeling horrible every hour of the day.
I was lucky enough to find StemGenex, and had the treatment here in the United States. My own stem cells were harvested from my adipose tissue, and re-introduced into my body thru IV, and localized injections.
I experienced no negative side effects! Within 24 hours, I started feeling much better, my balance started to return, I came home to do a yoga poise for my kids! Within in 3 months, my fog had cleared, my energy had increased. I was able to fix dinner for my kids....this may seem inconsequential to most, but to me, it was HUGE! I was off all medications, my depression had gone away, I had HOPE!!

I implore you to take the time to let those of us that have experienced the benefits of stem cell treatment to let us explain that this is the best possible treatment we have!! It has saved my insurance company tens of thousands in expensive medications. But most of all it has given me my life back! I am a mother and a wife again! My MRI's continue to show that since my stem cell therapy, I have had no new lesions in my brain or my spinal cord, and they have even shown slight re-myelination. Imagine if financially I could do this treatment more often!
Do I walk perfect, ...heck no, do I still have some minor symptoms, yes, but they are manageable. I am 51 years old and I still have MS, but I have shocked my doctors that I am still on my feet, and functioning. I know that with additional stem cell treatments, I can still continue to make improvements.

I want to ensure that others have the availability to have treatment, the current research is showing such positive results!!
Please do not take away my treatment options, and my HOPE for the future.

I've been lodging complaints with the FDA since 2012 on their mishandling of cellular therapy regulation. Glad to see some responsiveness, after our advocacy group Patients For Stem Cells helped drive a record turnout for the Part 15 hearing on these guidances. Over 600 registered, and 100 requested to speak, resulting in rescheduling. We are looking forward to productive exchange, in which the FDA helps facilitate accelerated access to this therapy, especially for no option patients like myself.

Every patient deserves the right to access this safe, life saving therapy NOW, not 10 years from now.

title: Comment from REGenableMED Consortium
comment_text:
Please find below comments on 'Draft Guidances Relating to the Regulation of Human Cells, Tissues, or Cellular or Tissue- Based Products; Public Hearing; Request for Comments' by the REGenableMED consortium.

REGenableMED - REGenableMED is a United Kingdom Economic and Social Research Council (ESRC)-funded project (NES/L002779/1: http://www.york.ac.uk/satsu/regenablemed/ ). It brings together research team builds on work by social science experts based in Birmingham, Edinburgh, Sussex and York in the UK. It is coordinated by Pr Andrew Webster, Science and Technology Studies Unit at the University of York, UK. The project aims to examine the dynamics of innovation within the field of regenerative medicine. Using a mixed-methods social science approach, the project will undertake a detailed analysis of the interplay between business models, measures of clinical utility, patterns of regulatory oversight and clinical workflows within healthcare settings. The results of the research will inform strategies aimed at facilitating the responsible development of effective and useful regenerative medicine products and services.

All work packages of the project consider what we call the 'institutional readiness', i. e. the capacity and willingness of key pre-existing organisations and inter-organisational structures to adopt, respond to and utilise novel technologies, such as advanced therapy medicinal products as part of regenerative medicine. One work package led by Prof Alex Faulkner, Centre for Global Health Policy, School of Global Studies, University of Sussex, the UK is dealing with the role of a range of intermediary agencies, patient groups and health insurance companies, in determining what can be called 'healthcare readiness' for the field, that is, how the field aligns with and can be embedded in existing practice and how far changes need to be made. As part of this work a regular survey of regulatory tools (including relevant linked public consultations) that influence the pathways through which the field develops is performed. The draft response has been prepared by Dr Aurlie Mahalatchimy (academic lawyer), Prof Alex Faulkner and Prof Andrew Webster (sociologists). A discussion between persons interested was then organised and the attached answer circulated to all project participants before submission.

The REGenableMED consortium is grateful to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to have been given the opportunity to contribute to this consultation.

COMMENTS

Minimal manipulation

-The FDA needs to clarify whether and if so at what point, a series or sequence of 'minimal' manipulations might be deemed to alter the relevant biological characteristics of cells or tissues? This is especially important, for example, for clinical researchers and companies developing bio-processing technologies as near-to-patient medical devices that are proposed as involving minimal manipulations.

Homologous use

Could you please clarify your guidance regarding bone marrow?

-How could bone marrow be regulated solely under section 361 of the PHS Act and 21 CFR Part 1271?
Indeed, to this end, it has to meet all of the criteria of 21 CFR 1271.10(a) (including to be "minimally manipulated", to be "intended for homologous use only" and its manufacture shall not "involve the combination of the cells or tissues with another article") while, by definition, "minimally manipulated bone marrow for homologous use and not combined with another article" is not considered HCT/P. (21 CFR 1271.3(d) (4))
-Moreover, an example is given of a non- homologous use of bone marrow: "HPCs derived from bone marrow are infused into an artery with a balloon catheter for the purpose of limiting ventricular remodeling following acute myocardial infarction. This is not homologous use because limiting ventricular remodeling is not a basic function of bone marrow." (page 5, 3-1 (b)).

REGenableMED - REGenableMED is a United Kingdom Economic and Social Research Council (ESRC)-funded project (NES/L002779/1: http://www.york.ac.uk/satsu/regenablemed/ ). It brings together research team builds on work by social science experts based in Birmingham, Edinburgh, Sussex and York in the UK. It is coordinated by Pr Andrew Webster, Science and Technology Studies Unit at the University of York, UK. The project aims to examine the dynamics of innovation within the field of regenerative medicine. Using a mixed-methods social science approach, the project will undertake a detailed analysis of the interplay between business models, measures of clinical utility, patterns of regulatory oversight and clinical workflows within healthcare settings. The results of the research will inform strategies aimed at facilitating the responsible development of effective and useful regenerative medicine products and services.

All work packages of the project consider what we call the 'institutional readiness', i. e. the capacity and willingness of key pre-existing organisations and inter-organisational structures to adopt, respond to and utilise novel technologies, such as advanced therapy medicinal products as part of regenerative medicine. One work package led by Prof Alex Faulkner, Centre for Global Health Policy, School of Global Studies, University of Sussex, the UK is dealing with the role of a range of intermediary agencies, patient groups and health insurance companies, in determining what can be called 'healthcare readiness' for the field, that is, how the field aligns with and can be embedded in existing practice and how far changes need to be made. As part of this work a regular survey of regulatory tools (including relevant linked public consultations) that influence the pathways through which the field develops is performed. The draft response has been prepared by Dr Aurlie Mahalatchimy (academic lawyer), Prof Alex Faulkner and Prof Andrew Webster (sociologists). A discussion between persons interested was then organised and the attached answer circulated to all project participants before submission.

The REGenableMED consortium is grateful to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to have been given the opportunity to contribute to this consultation.

Minimal manipulation

-The FDA needs to clarify whether and if so at what point, a series or sequence of 'minimal' manipulations might be deemed to alter the relevant biological characteristics of cells or tissues? title: Comment from James Newton
comment_text:
I am a recipient of stem cell therapy. I had a rotator cuff repair on my right shoulder (75% tear on one of the four muscles). My procedure was performed in Denver Colorado by the Centeno Shultz team of physicians. My results are both profound and impressive. I tried the regenerative approach because so many of my 40's and 50's friends had poor results from traditional surgery (more than half were not successful). The traditional recovery time was years, the traditional results were poor (range of motion not fully restored with any of the 6 people I know) and their quality of post-surgery life did not change.

Rotator Cuff - I tore my rotator cuff as a teen in high-school and it healed OK (I thought) until I was about 55. One day when working on my back in a basement crawl space with a pipe wrench in one hand, I re-injured the shoulder. It took weeks before my shoulder stopped hurting. It never did feel good at night. Eventually, I found that I could not sleep due to the shoulder pain and I consulted with these guys in Denver. I had read about them on the internet and seen something on one of the daytime TV shows. Several months before my visit to Denver, they took me off several medications that inhibit the platelet and stem cell injection effectiveness. They brought me into the clinic and looked at my shoulder. I was referred to an MRI associate who took some pictures of my shoulder. They looked again at my shoulder and determined that I was a good candidate. The overall process was efficient but expensive. The doctors took a week to poke my torn muscle with injections of saline and platelets to get it ready for the stem cell injection. Ultimately, some bone marrow from my hip was separated into a yellowish stem cells injection to my shoulder. They said they had to do all this stem cell stuff the same day because of FDA rules. If they could have taken more time to culture my stem cells, they have been seeing even greater success outside the US.

Well, my hip hurt, my shoulder hurt and I wasn't sure how well I would heal after a week in the clinic. At home - three weeks in the shoulder sling, I began feeling a change. Two months after the "injection surgery" I felt significantly better and could sleep for the first time in years. 6 months after injection surgery I had 80+ percent range of motion. Two years later (today) I have full range of motion and no scars or ill effects of this procedure. In the overall scheme of things, the $6000 up-front fee is significantly less than traditional rotator cuff costs my friends experienced. Also, I am near 100% range of motion, 95% strength and 90% pain free. I plan to return next year for a complete follow-up. This injection therapy seems too good to be true. What are you folks at the FDA looking at? Try looking at the results in patients. My un-healed friends only wish they could golf or even lift their arm above the head.

I am not a medical person but I have new respect for the efforts of the Centeno Shultz team. They have worked wonders for me. I don't know if the FDA even reads comments like this but I think they should. I only wish that I had a better background to tell you more technical details.

I was diagnosed with Multiple Sclerosis in May of 2001, at the age of 49. Through the years, even with prescription medicine, my body continued to decline. The injections destroyed muscle and tissue in my arms, legs, bottom, and stomach. Due to my condition, I had to take early retirement from teaching. The wheelchair became my main mode of transportation in public due to my lack of balance, speed, energy, mobility, and strength.

In hopes of improving my health, I tried to be part of MS trials in the United States and Canada. I was denied either because of my age, the clinics were not studying my specific symptoms, or the trials were closed to the public until they had studied the results for 10 years.

In 2011, I began stem cell treatments, through Celltex Therapeutics, in Houston, Texas. One deciding factor for me was that I could use my own adult stem cells. After extracting 2 teaspoons of fat cells from my stomach area, the cells were expanded in the lab over a 6 week period. I had the first in a series of treatments beginning in October of 2011, in Houston, receiving 200 million cells through an IV in my arm. I had a total of 8 treatments during 2011 and 2012, before the FDA stopped the treatments in the United States. The FDA now considers my own stem cells to be a drug since they are inserting a large number of my expanded cells back into my body.

Upon completing the first five of eight treatments I received in Houston, it was time for my yearly appointment with my neurologist. After performing the regular tests to assess my progress, as well as additional tests, Dr. Jackson shook his head and said, "You are not normal." When asked to clarify what he meant Dr. Jackson replied, "Your tests show that you are improving and that is not normal for your disease." His parting words that day were, "All I can say is you are better and I had nothing to do with it." Dr. Jackson and Dr. Patton continue to marvel at my improvements and have both given their blessings for further treatments.

Because the stem cell treatments were no longer available in the United States, I did not have treatments for 3 years. Fortunately, Celltex Therapeutics gained the approval of the Mexican equivalent of the FDA to continue treatments there. In May, 2015, my husband and I flew to Cancun, Mexico, in order for me to receive another series of treatments. In addition to 450 million stem cells received through 2 treatments of IVs in my arms, I also had 100 million stem cells infused in my spine and 50 million in each of two of the lymph nodes in my groin. I have had no negative side effects from these treatments. Each treatment offered additional healing.

* The wheelchair is no longer my main mode of transportation. I now use a walker unless I need to cover long distances in a short span of time.
* Body now tolerates hot and cold temperatures
* Renewed strength, energy, balance, and mobility

title: Comment from Paul Knoepfler
comment_text:
Dear FDA,
I'm writing to comment in support of your 4 recent draft guidances pertaining to HCT/Ps and in particular as they relate to investigational cell and specifically stem cell therapies. I urge you to finalize these draft guidances as soon as possible and importantly to begin taking regulatory action based upon them.

To me as a stem cell biologist interested in clinical translation and as someone who has been following the stem cell treatment field for a long time, my view is that the 4 draft guidances are positive steps that make good sense both from a common sense and scientific perspective.

More than minimally manipulated cellular products and those used in non-homologous fashion (these are common occurrences amongst the hundreds of stem cell clinics in the US today) pose greater risks to patients. More specifically, I don't see how adipose stem cells (aka fat stem cells, SVF) can be commonly used in a homologous fashion except in rare instances such as in tissues with a sizable normal adipose constituency. I also agree with the example in the draft guidance of SVF as a more than minimally manipulated product. There is in addition common, risky non-homologous use of bone marrow, blood or placental/amniotic cells amongst hundreds of American clinics from coast to coast.

As the US stem cell clinic industry continues to grow (I would predict there are more than 600 clinics selling non-FDA approved stem cell interventions today) there is an ever-growing need for clear, consistent, and proportionate regulatory oversight activity. To date we haven't seen that.

An industry this size largely operating without FDA approval or licensing of products via INDs and BLAs, is putting patients at great risk and it also jeopardizes the FDA's overall authority if the agency only takes minimal action (e.g. 1 or less warning letters per year from CBER). Finally, this situation poses serious risks to the exciting and promising legitimate stem cell and regenerative medicine field.

While advocates for clinics including some very sincere patients often invoke the importance of making 'their own' stem cells available to them and these can be very emotional and moving kinds of statements, the status quo of hundreds of clinics selling a hodge-podge of investigational stem cells to patients outside of the traditional clinical trial process is not benefiting the patients in any proven way and is instead putting them at sizable risk of harm.

For instance, in recent weeks we have heard about serious adverse events in patients who received unapproved stem cell interventions from clinics including a number of blinded patients and other adverse events have also occurred but are not yet in the public domain, making it all the more urgent that you approve the draft guidances and begin a period of proportionate regulatory activity related to stem cell clinics.

Thank you and best regards,
Paul Knoepfler
Professor
Cell Biology & Human Anatomy
UC Davis School of Medicine

title: Comment from Cell Surgical Network
comment_text:
Final version of comments presented at Sept 12, 2016 CBER meeting by Elliot Lander, Co-Medical Director, Cell Surgical Network

Cell Surgical Network represents over 400 physicians participating in nearly 100 multidisciplinary affiliated clinics around the world. Since 2010, CSN affiliates have safely performed over 5000 procedures under IRB protocols using our standardized same day cell surgery procedure with Autologous Adipose SVF or Stromal Vascular Fraction. Our patients receive proper pre-operative IRB informed consents and afterword, safety and efficacy data is collected online. Our data has been submitted for peer-review publication and also to the FDA. It is safe. There have been no deaths, infections, emboli or any severe adverse events related to cell therapy. It also works and improves many conditions where cellular repair is necessary. While collecting investigative data, we provide cell therapy for our patients in a low risk, cost effective, and transparent investigational manner often at reduced rates or even for free. We are making regenerative medicine available to Americans today through our SVF surgical procedure while we continue to gather data helping us to improve and advance patient care. This is the reason we became physicians.

While statements are frequently made claiming that such cell therapies are not FDA approved nor are such clinics performing them regulated, let us remember that the practice of medicine is already heavily regulated by State Medical Boards, hospital peer review committees, plaintiff's attorneys, and malpractice carriers. These regulations we address today were borne out of a congressional mandate to the FDA to prevent the introduction, transmission and spread of communicable disease. With jurisdiction over drugs and devices, the FDA has tried to define when our body parts come under their authority by considering Federal rules based on fat being only a cushion disregarding the science of what we know about fat. Technically, with the contemplated rules, the FDA would have broad sweeping jurisdiction over many traditional surgical procedures that don't strictly follow the new guidelines. We support guidelines giving the FDA the proper authority to ensure that we do not risk communicable disease introduction from outside sources, however, rules should not be used to infringe on a patient's right to surgical options using autologous tissue. Do we really want artificial and scientifically arbitrary guidance rules to dictate the course of any surgical procedure that violates the proposed list of exemptions? To date, there has never been an FDA approved surgical procedure. Further, same day surgical procedures providing autologous cell therapies, by their very nature are not fully closed systems and could never be held to the same standard as pharmacologically produced products. Medicine has historically been advanced by the wise tradition of allowing physicians to use any FDA approved drugs and devices in any way they see fit in order to advance innovation and help their patients.

While some oversight may be prudent, guidance document language should be reasonably flexible for physicians and their patients. Doctors should avoid irresponsible advertising or labelling claims not supported by data and state medical boards and a variety of agencies are already in place to counter deceptive advertising. CSN has endeavored to provide a transparent platform to gather real data. Reputable clinics will be easily comply with the registration process. Our database system can be recapitulated or licensed by regulators as a model for the ethical advancement of regenerative medicine. Such transparency would only serve the public by helping us advance protocols that work and eliminate ones that don't, paving the path for more controlled laboratory and clinical validation studies. But creating artificial and contrived rules that impact an entire nascent field of autologous SVF therapy will have unintended adverse consequences that will have epic ramifications - the FDA will be inadvertently selecting technology winners and losers that have little to do with safety and efficacy and more to do with semantics of guidelines proposals: the FDA will be complicit in criminalizing certain practices of medicine that are greatly supported by the American public despite a recent smear campaign intended to marginalize a new way of healing patients. Every day our Network team and the hundreds of doctors we do research with in the US and around the world are seeing things that we were told were impossible in medical school. If this wasn't real and safe, we'd all go back to our previous successful practices and autologous cell therapy would simply fade away. Clearly, that's not the case. Let patients and doctors decide. Let not special interests attempt to manipulate our distinguished regulatory agencies under the guise of protecting society.

I am a physician in practice for almost 40 years in South Florida. I had considerable knee problems with arthritis secondary to football injuries sustained when I was young. Two years ago for several months I started having considerable pain, nocturnal, in both knees significantly interfering with sleep necessitating narcotics and sleeping medicine. A person has some control of their own body and their cells , as per previous court action regarding HELA Cells , although not completely analogous their are some similarities.

I have no problem with the FDA promoting regulations and approval for the processing of the cells and the storage, freezing and defrosting of the cells, analogous to labs being certified, but I believe a person has a right to choose therapy that ONLY involves their own cells with no additional risk of rejection that they I doing with full recognition of the pros , cons and risks, with no third-party monies being involved.

I hopeyour decisions will increase the safety of this, not restrict the ability of patients to obtain a well needed therapeutic modality which they are paying for themselves. If youmake it to restrictive it will only force people to go overseas to facilities that are much less safe. I truly believe that research in the next several years will make this a standard therapeutic modality that will be accepted by insurance companies as the end cost of caring for the medical problem will probably be much less. Hopefully, your decisions will not restrict this until this eventuality occurs.

comment_text: Hello, I am a board certified medical doctor who in the past did not believe that homologous autologous stem cells could benefit my patients. However, after proper evaluation and treating 2 separate patients with conventional therapy for sever degenerative arthritis of the knees with nsaids, steroid injections and orthovisc, and failing to resolve their pain, I then scheduled them for knee replacement surgery. Both of these patients refused surgery and went to have autologous homologous stem cells injected in to their knees. When they returned to me for other medical problems I observed they did not require walkers to walk. I was unaware they had done stem cell therapy and asked how the surgeries had went. They proceeded to tell me how they did not do surgery but did stem cell therapy. I did not believe that it was actually stem cell therapy and I sternly interviewed them and realized they actually did have stem cell therapy. This was shocking to me because what happened to them NEVER occurs with there level of joint disease with out surgery to correct the problem. Being intrigued I looked for further research on the subject I found some good data in the European research which further supported stem cell success so I went and was trained on how to do autologous homologous stem cell procedures. I have now been providing theses treatment for the past 3 years and have had nearly a 90 % success rate at resolving numerous types of orthopedic disorders. The treatment population ranges in the age of 50 to 80 years old with all ethnic backgrounds and the severity of the their disease processes have all been in the sever category. I have treated around 300 patients. I have had no complications and no untoward affects of any of the procedures other than short term bruising from harvesting stem cells from the patients during the minimal invasive liposuction!!! Results such as I have experienced is to my knowledge NEVER seen with placebo affect. The nearly 90% of patients that had successful results have been followed and all of them have remained well over the course of the 3 years I have been doing this. Many of the 10 % that did not fully resolve their pain then went on to have orthopedic surgeries and not all of them were fully restored by surgery either. I know that homologous autologous stem cells harvested from the fat pad and re-injected with in the same day time frame is safe and very effective at treating orthopedic disease and has for at least the sever case patient has a better outcome rate than surgery. My recommendation is to continue to allow homologous autologous same day fat derived stem cell therapy to proceed under medical supervision with out restriction. There are some disorders which require repeat treatments every year or two . These diseases are autoimmune related disorders such as lupus, type one diabetes, dementia and multiple sclerosis. All of these disorders have had great success also with stem cell therapy but since the nature of the disease process is continual damage to the body any improvements made with stem cell will only last 1 to 2 years and would require repeat treatments. Under the current regulations banked stem cells can not be reintroduced unless the patient leaves the country to do so or to do repeat liposuction harvesting of fat derived stem cells in order to repeat therapy such as in the case for type one diabetes therapy. My second recommendation is to allow patients to be able to use their own stored stem cells for repeat procedures if needed. The benefits for alleviating suffering and having virtually no risk is a "no brainer" we must continue to allow patients to have access to this life saving procedure. From an economical stand point society as a whole will also greatly benefit from the low cost associated from autologous homologous stem cells. The cost of the procedure is low in relation to the cost of ongoing medical treatments such as daily medications, quarterly doctor visits to administer steroid injections and obviously the high cost of surgery with its associated risks and costly painful rehab. Please take in to consideration my two recommendations as elaborated in the above paragraph. Thank you for this opportunity to briefly express my concern. If needed you may contact me at www.nextgenerationstemcell.com

1 
 I am Suzanne O’Shea .  My comments are based on my experience as a long time FDA employee 
working with these issues, and 9 years of working with a number of tissue manufacturers in private 
practice.  My comments are my own, and do not represent the views of my employer or any client.  
 
I have five points  to make today.  
 
1.  The Draft Guidance on Minimal Manipulation introduces the concept of “main function for the very first 
time.  The concept does not  appear in Part 1271, or in any preamble to any proposed or final regulation.   
 
The Draft Guidance cites page 26749 of the preamble to the May 14, 1998 proposal as support for the 
assertion that the main function of the HCT/P in the donor determines which  definition of minimal 
manipulation applies.  However, the phrase “main function” is never used in the proposal .  The closest 
phrase on page 26749 is “basic function or functions ,” which is to be used in the contex t of determining 
homologous use.  
 
Creation of an important new concept ca nnot be done through guidance. I request that if FDA wishes to 
pursue the main function concept, it do so through notice and comment rulemaking.   
 
 
2. The Draft Guidance on Minimal Manipulation provides FDA’s unilateral concl usions on whether tissues 
are structural or non- structural.   
 
The guidance process does not provide a sufficient opportunity for industry and academia to provide input 
into the classification of tissues as structural or non- structural.  I recognize that c omments may be 
submitted on Draft Guidances, and I do appreciate this public hearing.  However, FDA is under no 
obligation to articulate a response to comments submitted to a Draft Guidance.  FDA is free to maintain 
its initial position without  explaining its reasoning.  
 I request that FDA’s classification of tissues as structural or non- structural be based on articulated 
reasoning that fully takes into account the views of industry and academia, through notice and comment 
rulemaking.  
 
 
3.  The Draft Guidance on Minimal Manipulation ignores the reality that some human tissues have both 
structural and non- structural functionality in the donor.   
 
I recommend that FDA expressly acknowledge the full range of functionality of human tissue in the donor, 
includin g the reality that som e tissues  have both structural and non- structural functionality.   
 
As a s pecific case in point, FDA stated in a 2001 designation letter that amniotic membrane has non-
structural anti-scarring, anti -inflammatory functionality  in the donor.  FDA now says, without any 
explanation why it has changed its mind, that amniotic membrane is only structural.  I recognize that a designation letter is intended for a specific product, and may not be applicable to all similar products.  
However, a s cientific conclusion about the functionality of a tissue in the donor  cannot vary based on the 
use of the tissue in the recipient.   
 
 
4.  The Draft Guidance on Homologous Use explicitly relies on the classification of a tissue as structural 
or non- structu ral to identify acceptable homologous uses.   
 
In creating the homologous use regulations, FDA considered and specifically rejected different definitions 
of homologous use for structural and non- structural tissues.  By importing the concept of “main functi on”  2 
 into the analysis of homologous use, FDA is limiting the range of acceptable homologous uses, contrary 
to current regulations.  
  
5.  FDA has applied the definition of minimal manipulation inconsistently, without explanation.   
 
FDA has concluded that micronized bone is a Section 361 product when intended for use as a bone void 
filler, even though micronization self -evidently alters the strength and compressibility of bone.  It must 
therefore be the case that FDA has concluded the strength and compressibility of bone are not relevant to 
bone’s utility as a bone void filler.  
 On the other hand, FDA has concluded that micronized amniotic membrane is more than minimally 
manipulated when intended for anti -scarring and anti -inflammator y uses, because tensile strength and 
elasticity are altered.  Tensile strength and elasticity are not relevant to the utility of amniotic membrane 
for anti -scarring and anti -inflammatory uses.   
 FDA has never explained this discrepancy.  I recommend that FDA provide a scientific explanation for the 
difference in treatment of micronized bone, and micronized amniotic membrane.   
 Thank you.

I have been treated successfully by adult stem cells. CellTex treated me while operating in Houston. The FDA shut down that clinic. I've since had to travel out of the country for treatment. The compassionate care and clnical trial options are not attainable for the vast majority of no option patients. As a no option patient with no FDA approved therapy to take, I should have the right to make a decision with my doctor to seek alternative treatment. Treatment with your own cells is a viable, safe option and should not be denied. There are years of use proving safety in adult stem cells. Currently 580+ clinics operating in the US with only 4 documented adverse reactions. I know the FDA approved drugs for MS have a much higher risk and mortality rate. If this is about patient safety, the numbers speak for themselves. The current system is failing chronically ill no option patients and must be changed.

[MANUAL ATTACHMENT TEXT]
Docket No. FDA –2015–D–3719 
“Draft Guidances Relating to the Regulation of Human Cells, Tissues, and 
cellular and tissue -based Products”  
I am responding to the request for comments regarding the recent FDA hearing 
regarding HCT/P’s. I am quite honestly appalled that it was necessary to have 
these hearings. There does not appear to be any reason for the FDA to be 
involved in this area. The p ractice of medicine is already thoroughly 
overseen by the Board of Medicine in each state. That the federal government 
would become involved in how doctors treat patients is redundant and 
confusing.  
Stem cell treatments have been given since the 1960’s in  the form of Bone 
Marrow transplants. Although they were very toxic initially, and not studied 
for decades, this procedure was given the opportunity to be developed and now 
is the standard of medicine. Over 50,000 patients have been treated with 
Adipose De rived Stem Cells, with barley an incident, yet this superior stem 
cell treatment is being subject to extraordinary scrutiny.  Over 100,000 
people die every year from taking antibiotics correctly, and these are FDA 
approved medications. There is not a singl e medication on the market that is 
as safe as mesenchymal stem cells.  If the procedure of obtaining stromal 
vascular fraction is required to have large, placebo  controlled , double -blind 
studies, then your intention must also be for all surgical procedures to 
undergo the same studies. This has never been done, and would be catastrophic 
for the practice of medicine.  
Patients should have the right to choose how they are treated. The 
opportunity to make informed decisions, based on fact is a patient right. 
When universities do not disclose the fact that they are a business, 
requiring the funding of pharmaceutical company’s grants, the reality of 
research is not as clear. Most people believe that the billions  of dollars 
given to universitie s is for the purpose o f improving/extending patient 
lives. This is, however, not the goal of most of these institutions, who 
rarely bring to market any product or procedure that directly impacts 
patients. In addition, university staff do not need to disclose this bias. 
When pat ients find that the best option for them is to have stem cell 
treatments, they should not be compelled to leave the country so that they 
can receive the most up to date therapies.  
That the FDA would consider labeling a patient’s own body tissue a drug is 
insulting. I should no more be told when, where, and how I may use my own 
body, than regulating what I eat. If I decide to have cookies for lunch, this 
may not be healthy or logical, but should not be illegal. We all require and 
appreciate the intervention of the FDA when we are discussing oversight of 
drugs, but this is not the case being discussed here.  
Thank you for your time.
